---
title: "Memento"
---

The **Memento** pattern captures and externalizes an object's internal state so it can be restored later, without violating encapsulation. It's like a game save system where you can checkpoint your progress and restore if you fail — the save file captures everything needed to restore your exact position.

## Problem

Imagine you're building a game with a save/load feature. The player has health, level, and position that need to be saved. The naive approach exposes all internal state, letting external code directly access and save it.

This leads to:

- Player's internal state is exposed (no encapsulation)
- SaveManager must know Player's internal structure
- If Player adds new fields, SaveManager must change
- No guarantee the saved data is consistent

### Example

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    SM[SaveManager] --> P["Player<br/>health (public)<br/>level (public)<br/>x, y (public)"]

    SM --> S["save = {<br/>health: player.health,<br/>level: player.level,<br/>...}"]

    style P fill:#fcc,stroke:#c33
    style S fill:#fcc,stroke:#c33
```

**Problems with this approach:**

- SaveManager directly accesses Player's fields
- Player has no control over what gets saved
- Adding new player state requires changing SaveManager
- No encapsulation — anyone can modify player state

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self.health = 100    # Public!
        self.level = 1       # Public!
        self.x = 0           # Public!
        self.y = 0           # Public!

    def take_damage(self, amount: int) -> None:
        self.health -= amount
        print(f"{self.name} took {amount} damage. Health: {self.health}")

    def move(self, x: int, y: int) -> None:
        self.x, self.y = x, y
        print(f"{self.name} moved to ({x}, {y})")

class SaveManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self.saves: list[dict] = []

    def save_game(self, player: Player) -> None:
        # Directly accessing player internals!
        save = {
            "health": player.health,
            "level": player.level,
            "x": player.x,
            "y": player.y,
        }
        self.saves.append(save)

    def load_game(self, player: Player, index: int) -> None:
        save = self.saves[index]
        # Directly modifying player internals!
        player.health = save["health"]
        player.level = save["level"]
        player.x = save["x"]
        player.y = save["y"]
```

#### `C#`

```csharp
public class Player
{
    public string Name { get; }
    public int Health { get; set; } = 100;    // Public setter!
    public int Level { get; set; } = 1;       // Public setter!
    public int X { get; set; } = 0;           // Public setter!
    public int Y { get; set; } = 0;           // Public setter!

    public Player(string name) => Name = name;

    public void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        Health -= amount;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} took {amount} damage. Health: {Health}");
    }

    public void Move(int x, int y)
    {
        X = x; Y = y;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} moved to ({x}, {y})");
    }
}

public class SaveManager
{
    private readonly List<Dictionary<string, int>> _saves = [];

    public void SaveGame(Player player)
    {
        // Directly accessing player internals!
        var save = new Dictionary<string, int>
        {
            ["health"] = player.Health,
            ["level"] = player.Level,
            ["x"] = player.X,
            ["y"] = player.Y
        };
        _saves.Add(save);
    }

    public void LoadGame(Player player, int index)
    {
        var save = _saves[index];
        // Directly modifying player internals!
        player.Health = save["health"];
        player.Level = save["level"];
        player.X = save["x"];
        player.Y = save["y"];
    }
}
```

#### `TypeScript`

```typescript
class Player {
  health: number = 100;    // Public!
  level: number = 1;       // Public!
  x: number = 0;           // Public!
  y: number = 0;           // Public!

  constructor(public name: string) {}

  takeDamage(amount: number): void {
    this.health -= amount;
    console.log(`${this.name} took ${amount} damage. Health: ${this.health}`);
  }

  move(x: number, y: number): void {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
    console.log(`${this.name} moved to (${x}, ${y})`);
  }
}

interface SaveData {
  health: number;
  level: number;
  x: number;
  y: number;
}

class SaveManager {
  private saves: SaveData[] = [];

  saveGame(player: Player): void {
    // Directly accessing player internals!
    const save: SaveData = {
      health: player.health,
      level: player.level,
      x: player.x,
      y: player.y,
    };
    this.saves.push(save);
  }

  loadGame(player: Player, index: number): void {
    const save = this.saves[index];
    // Directly modifying player internals!
    player.health = save.health;
    player.level = save.level;
    player.x = save.x;
    player.y = save.y;
  }
}
```

#### `Dart`

```dart
class Player {
  final String name;
  int health = 100;    // Public!
  int level = 1;       // Public!
  int x = 0;           // Public!
  int y = 0;           // Public!

  Player(this.name);

  void takeDamage(int amount) {
    health -= amount;
    print("$name took $amount damage. Health: $health");
  }

  void move(int newX, int newY) {
    x = newX;
    y = newY;
    print("$name moved to ($x, $y)");
  }
}

class SaveManager {
  final List<Map<String, int>> _saves = [];

  void saveGame(Player player) {
    // Directly accessing player internals!
    final save = {
      "health": player.health,
      "level": player.level,
      "x": player.x,
      "y": player.y,
    };
    _saves.add(save);
  }

  void loadGame(Player player, int index) {
    final save = _saves[index];
    // Directly modifying player internals!
    player.health = save["health"]!;
    player.level = save["level"]!;
    player.x = save["x"]!;
    player.y = save["y"]!;
  }
}
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
use std::collections::HashMap;

struct Player {
    pub name: String,
    pub health: i32, // Public!
    pub level: i32,  // Public!
    pub x: i32,      // Public!
    pub y: i32,      // Public!
}

impl Player {
    fn new(name: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            name: name.to_string(),
            health: 100,
            level: 1,
            x: 0,
            y: 0,
        }
    }

    fn take_damage(&mut self, amount: i32) {
        self.health -= amount;
        println!(
            "{} took {amount} damage. Health: {}",
            self.name, self.health
        );
    }

    // `move` is a Rust keyword, so the method is `move_to`
    fn move_to(&mut self, x: i32, y: i32) {
        (self.x, self.y) = (x, y);
        println!("{} moved to ({x}, {y})", self.name);
    }
}

struct SaveManager {
    saves: Vec<HashMap<&'static str, i32>>,
}

impl SaveManager {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { saves: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn save_game(&mut self, player: &Player) {
        // Directly accessing player internals!
        let save = HashMap::from([
            ("health", player.health),
            ("level", player.level),
            ("x", player.x),
            ("y", player.y),
        ]);
        self.saves.push(save);
    }

    fn load_game(&self, player: &mut Player, index: usize) {
        let save = &self.saves[index];
        // Directly modifying player internals!
        player.health = save["health"];
        player.level = save["level"];
        player.x = save["x"];
        player.y = save["y"];
    }
}
```

#### Usage

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
player = Player("Hero")
save_manager = SaveManager()

player.move(10, 20)
player.take_damage(30)
save_manager.save_game(player)  # Save checkpoint

player.take_damage(80)  # Oops, nearly dead!
print(f"Health before load: {player.health}")  # 0 or negative!

save_manager.load_game(player, 0)  # Restore
print(f"Health after load: {player.health}")   # 70

# Problem: SaveManager knows too much about Player's structure
# What if we add "mana" field? Must update SaveManager!
```

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut player = Player::new("Hero");
    let mut save_manager = SaveManager::new();

    player.move_to(10, 20);
    player.take_damage(30);
    save_manager.save_game(&player); // Save checkpoint

    player.take_damage(80); // Oops, nearly dead!
    println!("Health before load: {}", player.health); // 0 or negative!

    save_manager.load_game(&mut player, 0); // Restore
    println!("Health after load: {}", player.health); // 70

    // Problem: SaveManager knows too much about Player's structure
    // What if we add a "mana" field? Must update SaveManager!
}
```

:::


## Solution

The Memento pattern solves this by:

1. **Originator** (`Player`) creates mementos containing snapshots of its own state
2. **Memento** (`GameSave`) stores the state but keeps it private/opaque
3. **Caretaker** (`SaveManager`) stores mementos without examining their contents
4. Only the originator knows how to create and restore from mementos

The key insight: Player controls what gets saved and how it's restored. SaveManager is just a storage container.

### UML Diagram

```{mermaid}
classDiagram
    class Player {
        -health: int
        -level: int
        -x: int
        -y: int
        +save() GameSave
        +restore(save: GameSave)
        +takeDamage(amount: int)
        +move(x: int, y: int)
        +getStatus() String
    }

    class GameSave {
        -health: int
        -level: int
        -x: int
        -y: int
        -timestamp: DateTime
        +getTimestamp() DateTime
    }

    class SaveManager {
        -saves: List~GameSave~
        +addSave(save: GameSave)
        +getSave(index: int) GameSave
        +listSaves()
    }

    Player ..> GameSave : creates
    Player <.. GameSave : restores from
    SaveManager o--> GameSave : stores
```

### Refactored Code

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
from datetime import datetime

# Memento
class GameSave:
    def __init__(self, health: int, level: int, x: int, y: int):
        self._health = health
        self._level = level
        self._x = x
        self._y = y
        self._timestamp = datetime.now()

    def get_timestamp(self) -> datetime:
        return self._timestamp

    # State is "private" — only accessed by Player (friend relationship)

# Originator
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name: str):
        self.name = name
        self._health = 100
        self._level = 1
        self._x = 0
        self._y = 0

    def save(self) -> GameSave:
        """Create a memento with current state."""
        print(f"{self.name}: Game saved!")
        return GameSave(self._health, self._level, self._x, self._y)

    def restore(self, save: GameSave) -> None:
        """Restore state from a memento."""
        self._health = save._health
        self._level = save._level
        self._x = save._x
        self._y = save._y
        print(f"{self.name}: Game loaded from {save.get_timestamp()}")

    def take_damage(self, amount: int) -> None:
        self._health -= amount
        print(f"{self.name} took {amount} damage. Health: {self._health}")

    def move(self, x: int, y: int) -> None:
        self._x, self._y = x, y
        print(f"{self.name} moved to ({x}, {y})")

    def level_up(self) -> None:
        self._level += 1
        self._health = 100  # Restore health on level up
        print(f"{self.name} leveled up to {self._level}!")

    def get_status(self) -> str:
        return f"{self.name} [Lv.{self._level}] HP:{self._health} Pos:({self._x},{self._y})"

# Caretaker
class SaveManager:
    def __init__(self):
        self._saves: list[GameSave] = []

    def add_save(self, save: GameSave) -> None:
        self._saves.append(save)

    def get_save(self, index: int) -> GameSave:
        return self._saves[index]

    def list_saves(self) -> None:
        print("=== Save Slots ===")
        for i, save in enumerate(self._saves):
            print(f"  [{i}] {save.get_timestamp()}")
```

#### `C#`

```csharp
// Memento
public class GameSave
{
    internal int Health { get; }
    internal int Level { get; }
    internal int X { get; }
    internal int Y { get; }
    public DateTime Timestamp { get; }

    internal GameSave(int health, int level, int x, int y)
    {
        Health = health;
        Level = level;
        X = x;
        Y = y;
        Timestamp = DateTime.Now;
    }

    // State is internal — only accessible within the assembly
}

// Originator
public class Player
{
    public string Name { get; }
    private int _health = 100;
    private int _level = 1;
    private int _x = 0;
    private int _y = 0;

    public Player(string name) => Name = name;

    public GameSave Save()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name}: Game saved!");
        return new GameSave(_health, _level, _x, _y);
    }

    public void Restore(GameSave save)
    {
        _health = save.Health;
        _level = save.Level;
        _x = save.X;
        _y = save.Y;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name}: Game loaded from {save.Timestamp}");
    }

    public void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        _health -= amount;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} took {amount} damage. Health: {_health}");
    }

    public void Move(int x, int y)
    {
        _x = x; _y = y;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} moved to ({x}, {y})");
    }

    public void LevelUp()
    {
        _level++;
        _health = 100;
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} leveled up to {_level}!");
    }

    public string GetStatus() => $"{Name} [Lv.{_level}] HP:{_health} Pos:({_x},{_y})";
}

// Caretaker
public class SaveManager
{
    private readonly List<GameSave> _saves = [];

    public void AddSave(GameSave save) => _saves.Add(save);

    public GameSave GetSave(int index) => _saves[index];

    public void ListSaves()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("=== Save Slots ===");
        for (int i = 0; i < _saves.Count; i++)
            Console.WriteLine($"  [{i}] {_saves[i].Timestamp}");
    }
}
```

#### `TypeScript`

```typescript
// Memento
class GameSave {
  private readonly health: number;
  private readonly level: number;
  private readonly x: number;
  private readonly y: number;
  private readonly timestamp: Date;

  constructor(health: number, level: number, x: number, y: number) {
    this.health = health;
    this.level = level;
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
    this.timestamp = new Date();
  }

  getTimestamp(): Date {
    return this.timestamp;
  }

  // Expose state only to Player (via package/friend access in real scenario)
  getState(): { health: number; level: number; x: number; y: number } {
    return { health: this.health, level: this.level, x: this.x, y: this.y };
  }
}

// Originator
class Player {
  private health: number = 100;
  private level: number = 1;
  private x: number = 0;
  private y: number = 0;

  constructor(public readonly name: string) {}

  save(): GameSave {
    console.log(`${this.name}: Game saved!`);
    return new GameSave(this.health, this.level, this.x, this.y);
  }

  restore(save: GameSave): void {
    const state = save.getState();
    this.health = state.health;
    this.level = state.level;
    this.x = state.x;
    this.y = state.y;
    console.log(`${this.name}: Game loaded from ${save.getTimestamp()}`);
  }

  takeDamage(amount: number): void {
    this.health -= amount;
    console.log(`${this.name} took ${amount} damage. Health: ${this.health}`);
  }

  move(x: number, y: number): void {
    this.x = x;
    this.y = y;
    console.log(`${this.name} moved to (${x}, ${y})`);
  }

  levelUp(): void {
    this.level++;
    this.health = 100;
    console.log(`${this.name} leveled up to ${this.level}!`);
  }

  getStatus(): string {
    return `${this.name} [Lv.${this.level}] HP:${this.health} Pos:(${this.x},${this.y})`;
  }
}

// Caretaker
class SaveManager {
  private saves: GameSave[] = [];

  addSave(save: GameSave): void {
    this.saves.push(save);
  }

  getSave(index: number): GameSave {
    return this.saves[index];
  }

  listSaves(): void {
    console.log("=== Save Slots ===");
    this.saves.forEach((save, i) => {
      console.log(`  [${i}] ${save.getTimestamp()}`);
    });
  }
}
```

```dart
  void addSave(GameSave save) => _saves.add(save);

  GameSave getSave(int index) => _saves[index];
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
// Rust privacy is per module: Memento and Originator share `mod game`
mod game {
    use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

    // Memento → `pub` type, private fields
    pub struct GameSave {
        health: i32,
        level: i32,
        x: i32,
        y: i32,
        timestamp: u64, // seconds since the Unix epoch (std has no date formatting)
    }

    impl GameSave {
        // The only thing the caretaker may read
        pub fn get_timestamp(&self) -> u64 {
            self.timestamp
        }
    }

    // Originator → in the same module, so it can read GameSave's private fields
    pub struct Player {
        name: String,
        health: i32,
        level: i32,
        x: i32,
        y: i32,
    }

    impl Player {
        pub fn new(name: &str) -> Self {
            Self {
                name: name.to_string(),
                health: 100,
                level: 1,
                x: 0,
                y: 0,
            }
        }

        /// Create a memento with current state.
        pub fn save(&self) -> GameSave {
            println!("{}: Game saved!", self.name);
            let timestamp = SystemTime::now()
                .duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)
                .map_or(0, |elapsed| elapsed.as_secs());
            GameSave {
                health: self.health,
                level: self.level,
                x: self.x,
                y: self.y,
                timestamp,
            }
        }

        /// Restore state from a memento.
        pub fn restore(&mut self, save: &GameSave) {
            self.health = save.health;
            self.level = save.level;
            self.x = save.x;
            self.y = save.y;
            println!("{}: Game loaded from {}", self.name, save.get_timestamp());
        }

        pub fn take_damage(&mut self, amount: i32) {
            self.health -= amount;
            println!(
                "{} took {amount} damage. Health: {}",
                self.name, self.health
            );
        }

        // `move` is a Rust keyword, so the method is `move_to`
        pub fn move_to(&mut self, x: i32, y: i32) {
            (self.x, self.y) = (x, y);
            println!("{} moved to ({x}, {y})", self.name);
        }

        pub fn level_up(&mut self) {
            self.level += 1;
            self.health = 100; // Restore health on level up
            println!("{} leveled up to {}!", self.name, self.level);
        }

        pub fn get_status(&self) -> String {
            format!(
                "{} [Lv.{}] HP:{} Pos:({},{})",
                self.name, self.level, self.health, self.x, self.y
            )
        }
    }
}

use game::{GameSave, Player};

// Caretaker → outside `mod game`: it stores saves but cannot read their fields
struct SaveManager {
    saves: Vec<GameSave>,
}

impl SaveManager {
    fn new() -> Self {
        Self { saves: Vec::new() }
    }

    fn add_save(&mut self, save: GameSave) {
        self.saves.push(save);
    }

    fn get_save(&self, index: usize) -> &GameSave {
        &self.saves[index]
    }

    fn list_saves(&self) {
        println!("=== Save Slots ===");
        for (i, save) in self.saves.iter().enumerate() {
            println!("  [{i}] {}", save.get_timestamp());
            // save.health → ❌ error[E0616]: field `health` of struct `GameSave` is private
        }
    }
}
```

#### Usage

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
player = Player("Hero")
save_manager = SaveManager()

# Play the game
player.move(10, 20)
player.take_damage(30)
print(player.get_status())
# Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

# Create a save point
save_manager.add_save(player.save())

# Continue playing...
player.move(50, 50)
player.take_damage(80)  # Almost dead!
print(player.get_status())
# Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

# Restore from save

player.restore(save_manager.get_save(0))
print(player.get_status())
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="🦀 Rust lens"}
| GoF role | Rust |
|---|---|
| Memento | `pub struct GameSave` with private fields, inside `mod game` |
| Originator | `Player` in the same module: it reads `GameSave`'s private fields, like a C++ `friend` |
| Caretaker | `SaveManager` outside the module: it stores `GameSave` values but cannot read their fields |
| Narrow interface for the caretaker | `get_timestamp()`, the only `pub` method on `GameSave` |
| Save / restore | `save(&self) -> GameSave` builds a new value; `restore(&mut self, &GameSave)` borrows one |

**Ownership:** privacy in Rust is per module, not per type, and that is exactly what Memento needs. Put the originator and the memento in one module and the caretaker outside it. The compiler then enforces the "opaque to the caretaker" rule that Python leaves to the `_` convention (`save.health` in `SaveManager` is error E0616). `SaveManager` owns its saves, and `get_save()` lends one out as `&GameSave`, so a restore copies no save. See the [OOP Cheatsheet](../oop/oop-cheatsheet.qmd#rust) for the general mapping.
:::

## Modern Approach

Model the player's state as one **immutable value** and the memento disappears into it. Every state is already a snapshot. Saving returns the current value with no copy, restoring is one assignment, and the caretaker is a plain list. The trade-off is encapsulation: a snapshot is now readable by anyone, though nobody can change it. Rust reaches the same place from the other side. A `Copy` struct is copied on every assignment, so a saved snapshot never aliases the live state, and the player can even change its state in place.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Verdict: 🟡 Simplifies** — immutable state makes every state its own memento, but the originator still decides what that state contains.
:::

### Feature Map

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `class GameSave` copying `_health`, `_level`, `_x`, `_y` | `@dataclass(frozen=True) class PlayerState`: the state *is* the snapshot |
| Four private fields on `Player` | one `_state` field, replaced via `dataclasses.replace()` |
| `save()` copies fields into a new `GameSave` | `save()` returns `self._state`: it's immutable, so no copy |
| `restore()` copies fields back | `restore()` assigns one reference |
| `class SaveManager` (caretaker) | a plain `list[PlayerState]` |
| State "hidden" by the `_` naming convention | readable by anyone, but writes raise `FrozenInstanceError` |

#### `C#`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `class GameSave` with `internal` getters | `record PlayerState(int Health = 100, …)` |
| Four private fields on `Player` | one `_state` field, replaced with a `with` expression |
| `Save()` copies into `new GameSave(…)` | `Save()` returns `_state`: it's immutable, so no copy |
| `Restore()` copies fields back | `Restore()` assigns one reference |
| `class SaveManager` (caretaker) | a plain `List<PlayerState>` |
| `internal` hides state outside the assembly | public, but `init`-only properties reject writes |

#### `TypeScript`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `class GameSave` with private fields + `getState()` | `type PlayerState = Readonly<{ … }>` |
| Four private fields on `Player` | one `state` field, replaced with object spread |
| `save()` copies into `new GameSave(…)` | `save()` returns `this.state`: it's immutable, so no copy |
| `restore()` copies fields back | `restore()` assigns one reference |
| `class SaveManager` (caretaker) | a plain `PlayerState[]` |
| `getState()` exposes the state anyway | readable; `readonly` blocks writes at compile time (add `Object.freeze` for runtime) |

#### `Dart`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `class GameSave` with private fields + public getters | immutable `PlayerState` with `final` fields + `copyWith()` |
| Four private fields on `Player` | one `_state` field, replaced via `copyWith()` |
| `save()` copies into `GameSave(…)` | `save()` returns `_state`: it's immutable, so no copy |
| `restore()` copies fields back | `restore()` assigns one reference |
| `class SaveManager` (caretaker) | a plain `List<PlayerState>` |
| Public getters expose the state anyway | readable, but `final` fields reject writes |

#### `Rust`

| Classic | Modern |
|---|---|
| `struct GameSave` copying `health`, `level`, `x`, `y` | `#[derive(Clone, Copy)] struct PlayerState`: the state *is* the snapshot |
| Four private fields on `Player` | one `state: PlayerState` field, changed in place (`self.state.health -= amount`) |
| `save()` builds a new `GameSave` | `save()` returns `self.state`: `Copy` gives the caller its own snapshot |
| `restore(&GameSave)` copies fields back | `restore(snapshot)` is one assignment |
| `struct SaveManager` (caretaker) | a plain `Vec<PlayerState>` |
| `mod game` privacy hides the memento's fields | readable by anyone, and a write changes only that copy: values never alias |

:::

**Ecosystem:** Immer (`produceWithPatches` / `applyPatches`) stores undo history as small patches instead of full snapshots, and Redux-style stores keep past states for time travel. Dart's `freezed` generates `copyWith`. To persist a save to disk, serialize the snapshot (`json`, `System.Text.Json`, `JSON.stringify`, `json_serializable`, Rust's `serde`).

### Modern Code

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### `Python`

```python
# Python 3.10+ — frozen dataclass snapshots, dataclasses.replace
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


# Memento → the player's state itself, as an immutable value
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PlayerState:
    health: int = 100
    level: int = 1
    x: int = 0
    y: int = 0


# Originator → holds one state value and swaps it on every change
class Player:
    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name
        self._state = PlayerState()

    def save(self) -> PlayerState:
        print(f"{self.name}: Game saved!")
        return self._state  # no copy needed: nobody can mutate it

    def restore(self, snapshot: PlayerState) -> None:
        self._state = snapshot
        print(f"{self.name}: Game loaded")

    def take_damage(self, amount: int) -> None:
        self._state = replace(self._state, health=self._state.health - amount)
        print(f"{self.name} took {amount} damage. Health: {self._state.health}")

    def move(self, x: int, y: int) -> None:
        self._state = replace(self._state, x=x, y=y)
        print(f"{self.name} moved to ({x}, {y})")

    def get_status(self) -> str:
        s = self._state
        return f"{self.name} [Lv.{s.level}] HP:{s.health} Pos:({s.x},{s.y})"


# --- Usage ---
player = Player("Hero")
saves: list[PlayerState] = []  # Caretaker → a plain list

player.move(10, 20)
player.take_damage(30)
print(player.get_status())  # Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

saves.append(player.save())  # Hero: Game saved!

player.move(50, 50)
player.take_damage(80)
print(player.get_status())  # Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

player.restore(saves[0])  # Hero: Game loaded
print(player.get_status())  # Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

# The caretaker CAN read a snapshot, but can't change it
print(f"Slot 0 health: {saves[0].health}")  # Slot 0 health: 70
# saves[0].health = 999  → FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'health'
```

```csharp
// C# 10+ / .NET 8+ — positional record snapshots, `with` expressions

// Memento → the player's state itself, as an immutable record
public record PlayerState(int Health = 100, int Level = 1, int X = 0, int Y = 0);

// Originator → holds one state value and swaps it on every change
public class Player(string name)
{
    private PlayerState _state = new();

    public PlayerState Save()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{name}: Game saved!");
        return _state;  // no copy needed: nobody can mutate it
    }

    public void Restore(PlayerState snapshot)
    {
        _state = snapshot;
        Console.WriteLine($"{name}: Game loaded");
    }

    public void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        _state = _state with { Health = _state.Health - amount };
        Console.WriteLine($"{name} took {amount} damage. Health: {_state.Health}");
    }

    public void Move(int x, int y)
    {
        _state = _state with { X = x, Y = y };
        Console.WriteLine($"{name} moved to ({x}, {y})");
    }

    public string GetStatus() =>
        $"{name} [Lv.{_state.Level}] HP:{_state.Health} Pos:({_state.X},{_state.Y})";
}

// --- Usage ---

var saves = new List<PlayerState>();  // Caretaker → a plain list

player.Move(10, 20);
player.TakeDamage(30);
Console.WriteLine(player.GetStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

saves.Add(player.Save());  // Hero: Game saved!

player.Move(50, 50);
player.TakeDamage(80);
Console.WriteLine(player.GetStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

player.Restore(saves[0]);  // Hero: Game loaded
Console.WriteLine(player.GetStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

// The caretaker CAN read a snapshot, but can't change it
Console.WriteLine($"Slot 0 health: {saves[0].Health}");  // Slot 0 health: 70
// saves[0].Health = 999;  → CS8852: Init-only property or indexer 'PlayerState.Health' can only be assigned in an object initializer…
```

```typescript
// TypeScript 5.x — readonly snapshot types, object spread

// Memento → the player's state itself, as an immutable value
type PlayerState = Readonly<{ health: number; level: number; x: number; y: number }>;

// Originator → holds one state value and swaps it on every change
class Player {
  readonly name: string;
  private state: PlayerState = { health: 100, level: 1, x: 0, y: 0 };

  constructor(name: string) {
    this.name = name;
  }

  save(): PlayerState {
    console.log(`${this.name}: Game saved!`);
    return this.state;  // no copy needed: nobody can mutate it
  }

  restore(snapshot: PlayerState): void {
    this.state = snapshot;
    console.log(`${this.name}: Game loaded`);
  }

  takeDamage(amount: number): void {
    this.state = { ...this.state, health: this.state.health - amount };
    console.log(`${this.name} took ${amount} damage. Health: ${this.state.health}`);
  }

  move(x: number, y: number): void {
    this.state = { ...this.state, x, y };
    console.log(`${this.name} moved to (${x}, ${y})`);
  }

  getStatus(): string {
    const s = this.state;
    return `${this.name} [Lv.${s.level}] HP:${s.health} Pos:(${s.x},${s.y})`;
  }
}

// --- Usage ---
const player = new Player("Hero");
const saves: PlayerState[] = [];  // Caretaker → a plain array

player.move(10, 20);
player.takeDamage(30);
console.log(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

saves.push(player.save());  // Hero: Game saved!

player.move(50, 50);
player.takeDamage(80);
console.log(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

player.restore(saves[0]);  // Hero: Game loaded
console.log(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

// The caretaker CAN read a snapshot, but can't change it
console.log(`Slot 0 health: ${saves[0].health}`);  // Slot 0 health: 70
// saves[0].health = 999;  → TS2540: Cannot assign to 'health' because it is a read-only property
```

```dart
// Dart 3.x — immutable class with final fields + copyWith

// Memento → the player's state itself, as an immutable value
class PlayerState {
  final int health;
  final int level;
  final int x;
  final int y;

  const PlayerState({this.health = 100, this.level = 1, this.x = 0, this.y = 0});

  // Hand-written here; `freezed` generates it in real projects
  PlayerState copyWith({int? health, int? level, int? x, int? y}) => PlayerState(
        health: health ?? this.health,
        level: level ?? this.level,
        x: x ?? this.x,
        y: y ?? this.y,
      );
}

// Originator → holds one state value and swaps it on every change
class Player {
  final String name;
  PlayerState _state = const PlayerState();

  Player(this.name);

  PlayerState save() {
    print("$name: Game saved!");
    return _state;  // no copy needed: nobody can mutate it
  }

  void restore(PlayerState snapshot) {
    _state = snapshot;
    print("$name: Game loaded");
  }

  void takeDamage(int amount) {
    _state = _state.copyWith(health: _state.health - amount);
    print("$name took $amount damage. Health: ${_state.health}");
  }

  void move(int x, int y) {
    _state = _state.copyWith(x: x, y: y);
    print("$name moved to ($x, $y)");
  }

  String getStatus() =>
      "$name [Lv.${_state.level}] HP:${_state.health} Pos:(${_state.x},${_state.y})";
}

// --- Usage ---
void main() {
  final player = Player("Hero");
  final saves = <PlayerState>[];  // Caretaker → a plain list

  player.move(10, 20);
  player.takeDamage(30);
  print(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

  saves.add(player.save());  // Hero: Game saved!

  player.move(50, 50);
  player.takeDamage(80);
  print(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

  player.restore(saves[0]);  // Hero: Game loaded
  print(player.getStatus());  // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

  // The caretaker CAN read a snapshot, but can't change it
  print("Slot 0 health: ${saves[0].health}");  // Slot 0 health: 70
  // saves[0].health = 999;  → 'health' can't be used as a setter because it's final
}
```

#### `Rust`

```rust
// Rust 1.85+ (edition 2024) — Copy structs as snapshots
// Memento → the player's state itself, as a plain `Copy` value
#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
struct PlayerState {
    health: i32,
    level: i32,
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}

impl Default for PlayerState {
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            health: 100,
            level: 1,
            x: 0,
            y: 0,
        }
    }
}

// Originator → holds one state value. Mutating it in place is safe:
// every saved snapshot is a separate copy, so nothing aliases the live state.
struct Player {
    name: String,
    state: PlayerState,
}

impl Player {
    fn new(name: &str) -> Self {
        Self {
            name: name.to_string(),
            state: PlayerState::default(),
        }
    }

    fn save(&self) -> PlayerState {
        println!("{}: Game saved!", self.name);
        self.state // `Copy`: the caller gets its own snapshot
    }

    fn restore(&mut self, snapshot: PlayerState) {
        self.state = snapshot;
        println!("{}: Game loaded", self.name);
    }

    fn take_damage(&mut self, amount: i32) {
        self.state.health -= amount;
        println!(
            "{} took {amount} damage. Health: {}",
            self.name, self.state.health
        );
    }

    fn move_to(&mut self, x: i32, y: i32) {
        (self.state.x, self.state.y) = (x, y);
        println!("{} moved to ({x}, {y})", self.name);
    }

    fn get_status(&self) -> String {
        let s = self.state;
        format!(
            "{} [Lv.{}] HP:{} Pos:({},{})",
            self.name, s.level, s.health, s.x, s.y
        )
    }
}

// --- Usage ---
fn main() {
    let mut player = Player::new("Hero");
    let mut saves: Vec<PlayerState> = Vec::new(); // Caretaker → a plain Vec

    player.move_to(10, 20);
    player.take_damage(30);
    println!("{}", player.get_status()); // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

    saves.push(player.save()); // Hero: Game saved!

    player.move_to(50, 50);
    player.take_damage(80);
    println!("{}", player.get_status()); // Hero [Lv.1] HP:-10 Pos:(50,50)

    player.restore(saves[0]); // Hero: Game loaded
    println!("{}", player.get_status()); // Hero [Lv.1] HP:70 Pos:(10,20)

    // The caretaker CAN read a snapshot. A write would change only its own copy,
    // never the player: snapshots and live state never alias.
    println!("Slot 0 health: {}", saves[0].health); // Slot 0 health: 70
}
```

:::

### Classic or Modern?

| Prefer immutable snapshots when | Keep a classic memento when |
|---|---|
| State is small, plain data | State holds things you can't share or copy cheaply: open files, sockets, large buffers |
| You want undo/redo as a simple list of past states | The snapshot must stay opaque to the caretaker (a narrow interface), e.g. across a plugin API |
| The object is already modeled as a value (Redux, Bloc, or Elm style) | Saves need a custom format or only a delta, e.g. save files that must survive version upgrades |
| Rust: the state is plain data, so `#[derive(Clone)]` or `Copy` makes snapshots for free | Rust: the state holds a value with no `Clone` (a `File`, a socket), and the compiler refuses to copy it |

## Summary

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" collapse="false"}
**Memento** captures an object's internal state in a snapshot that can be restored later, without exposing the object's internal structure.
:::

### Key Benefits

- **Encapsulation Preserved**: Internal state stays private; only the originator knows the structure
- **Clean Separation**: Caretaker stores mementos without knowing their contents
- **Unlimited Snapshots**: Can save multiple checkpoints, restore any of them
- **Simplified Undo**: Perfect for implementing undo/rollback functionality
- **Consistent State**: Originator ensures memento captures a valid, complete snapshot

### Memento vs Command Pattern

| Aspect | Memento | Command |
|--------|---------|---------|
| **Focus** | Snapshot of complete state | Individual operations |
| **Undo** | Restore entire state | Reverse the operation |
| **Storage** | Stores full snapshots | Stores operation + delta |
| **Use Case** | Checkpoints, save games | Operation history, transactions |

### When to Use

| ✅ Use When | ❌ Avoid When |
|------------|--------------|
| You need to save/restore an object's complete state | State is simple enough to copy directly |
| You want to implement checkpoints or save games | Mementos would consume too much memory |
| You need to preserve encapsulation while saving state | The originator's state changes frequently |
| You want undo functionality without exposing internals | You only need to undo specific operations (use Command) |
